title: Nostalgia and addiction
content_html:
Nostalgia and addiction: The past had better drugs.

If somebody you love is suffering with an addiction, you’ll know that they are sensitive. They’re more susceptible to the maelstrom of emotions than others. They have a beautiful light inside, that gets dulled through the dark that drags over them. Sometimes it can seem like the light has entirely left. But it’s still in there, somewhere, flickering defiantly against the forces that want it to die. They’re often very talented, but are the last ones to believe in themselves. The most ambitious people I’ve ever known, are people who’ve overcome an addiction. Once you’ve been through your own personal hell, everything else becomes a walk in the park.

If you know an addict, there is a storm in their chest, and they’re wearing the wrong clothes for the weather. Trying to distract themselves from the looming emptiness that stalks, is like putting your hand over a volcano to stop the lava. Eventually it’ll erupt over everyone they love. And the destruction they leave in their wake, could reshape entire cities. Sometimes life can seem like a monument of loss. Sometimes the abyss has magnets inside it. Sometimes we see the label and miss the small print, but drink the bottle anyway.

Beyond genetic and environmental factors, I think there is a huge crossover between addiction and nostalgia. Those who experience addiction put the past on a pedestal and romanticise it. They chase shadows that seem taller than they are. They feel warm bliss with a selective memory, a highlight reel of a speckled past. In recovery circles, this is known as “euphoric recall”—when the brain edits the archive, and you only remember the moments of connection: the first time you took an ecstasy pill, rather than crawling around your bedroom on all fours at 7am, sniffing anything off the ground that looks like coke (it was lint.) And this, gives us a useful insight about nostalgia—we don’t want to return to the past as it was, we want to return to a cherry-picked, de-contextualised, de-politicised version of it. We want the rose-tinted aroma to overpower the shit that we smelt, we want the memories of pleasure to paint over the pain. So in our minds, we build our home with no blinkers on, re-mapping the demolition site into utopia.

If you talk to someone who relapses into substance use or addictive behaviour again, and ask them why they did it, they’ll usually tell you (and we could say it in unison) “I thought it would be different this time.” Their belief, and attempt to recreate the good times before the consequences piled up on them, bypasses all logic and evidence that suggests it’s a bad idea to go back to the good old days. And these people are not stupid, they are seduced. Nostalgia, like a drug of its own—whispers in a language that feels like our voice. It offers a warm escape from our troubles, it frees us of responsibility and allows us to forget the anxieties of the future. So we dive headfirst into the back of our minds, weaving a happy home out of a tangled mess, to escape from a life without practice runs.

For those who experience addiction, there’s too much past in their present, so they can’t live in the moment. There’s an uncanny similarity here too—take an alcoholic who has to be sober for a family event; they’ll usually be watching the clock, not able to take anything in, and will be counting down the minutes they can leave for a drink. Nostalgia here, has a similar function. It stops us from activating change in the present, and showing up for life in the way that we should. And on a sociological level, nostalgia is akin to an escape back into the womb, we yearn for utero, when we drink to oblivion, we are seeking annihilation of the self; for a time before our time began. We want the sweet isolation of an unaccountable life. And the only way to achieve it is to overshoot.

When we zoom out of addiction for a moment, nostalgia is a defence mechanism. It’s a protective shell against a world that moves too fast. Technology accelerates at breakneck pace, while culture gets stuck in a bottleneck. When our bodies are pulled towards endless distractions, peppered with outrage porn and things we should care about—we experience an overwhelm like never before; where information is abundant, but we don’t have the bandwidth to pay attention to it. When the present doesn’t hold shape, and the world gives us whiplash, we turn our heads to yesterday, so we run backwards, and grow in reverse, like budding flowers moving towards the light of the moon. When life draws circles around our tired eyelids, we want to spin around in fields with no phone in our pockets.

Maybe having a sensitivity to addiction, is having a sensitivity to nostalgia. And while it’s an emotion we’re all susceptible to, for those with a drug dependency, nostalgia can be fatal. Maybe if we lived in a world where the present wasn’t unstable, and we felt anchored to something lasting and real, we wouldn’t have to look to the past for comfort and escape. Nostalgia is a rational response to a world that’s accelerated out of control. And we’ve all got track-marks on our arms.

The question is: how do we build a life people don’t need nostalgia to escape out of? How do we create enough hospital beds for childhood wounds, and a sun that shines on our dark parts when we don’t think we deserve it? How do we find community when competition tells us we’re in it alone? How do we afford a home that we would like to live in? How do we race to the bottom and throw a street party at the finish line? How do we create a world we want to get out of bed for? These may seem like insurmountable obstacles alone, but together, if we can decorate the present with little reasons to stay, then the past wouldn’t reel us into a relapse.
